analysis.one_liner: Makes employers legally responsible for workplace harassment by bosses who direct a worker's daily job.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or vote before the 114th Congress ended, dying in the Senate HELP Committee with 10 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change who counts as a "supervisor" in workplace harassment lawsuits. In 2013, the Supreme Court ruled in Vance v. Ball State University that an employer is only automatically liable for harassment by someone with the power to hire, fire, or demote the victim — not by a shift leader who simply directs the worker's day-to-day tasks. The bill would overturn that ruling, making employers liable when a harasser either could take or recommend tangible employment actions, could direct the worker's daily activities, or when the employer's own negligence allowed the harassment to continue. It would apply the same standard across federal civil rights, age, disability, and genetic-discrimination employment laws, including harassment of Congressional employees.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are harassed by someone with day-to-day authority over them — a shift supervisor, crew leader, or charge nurse — even if that person cannot formally hire or fire them. The bill's findings single out workers in retail, restaurants, health care, housekeeping, farm work, and personal care, where low pay and high shares of female workers coincide with harassers who control daily work but lack formal hiring-and-firing power [S3]. Workers who currently lose cases because of the Vance ruling would regain a path to hold the employer responsible [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers harassed by bosses who direct daily work

how_it_helps.text: Restores strict employer liability for harassment by anyone authorized to undertake or recommend tangible employment actions OR to direct the employee's daily work activities, reversing the narrower supervisor definition the Supreme Court set in Vance v. Ball State University [S2][S3].

Adds an independent negligence standard: an employer is liable whenever its own negligence led to the creation or continuation of the hostile work environment, closing routes to liability that the Vance-era defense framework made easier to escape [S3].

Applies the standard across Title VII (sex, race, religion, national origin), the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the ADA, the Rehabilitation Act, section 1981, the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act, the Government Employee Rights Act, executive-branch employment law, and the Congressional Accountability Act — including employees of Congress itself [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers — particularly those in low-wage industries with many first-line supervisors who lack formal hiring-and-firing authority — would face broader liability in harassment lawsuits, including cases where a worker harassed by a shift leader never had to prove the employer was negligent. Insurers and litigation defense costs would rise accordingly.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies to claims pending on or after enactment, meaning it would reach ongoing lawsuits and expose employers to liability under the new standard immediately rather than prospectively [S3].

Critics of the pre-Vance standard argued that it counts millions of employees as "supervisors" for liability purposes even when they have no real authority over pay or employment decisions, which employers said increases the cost of defending workplace claims without reducing actual harassment. The bill keeps the Faragher/Ellertb employer defenses available (Section 12 preserves existing defenses) but expands the class of harassers for whom strict liability applies [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a well-documented gap: after the Vance ruling, workers harassed by people with real day-to-day power over their schedules, assignments, and conditions often cannot hold the employer responsible. That gap falls hardest on low-wage, majority-female workforces named in the bill's own findings. The cost falls on employers as expanded legal exposure and higher harassment insurance and defense costs; whether that cost produces better workplace conduct or merely transfers money in litigation is the honest open question. The bill is narrow and targeted — it changes one liability standard across existing statutes rather than creating new claims or penalties.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee took no further action on it before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced June 23, 2016 by Sen. Tammy Baldwin with nine Senate Democrats as original cosponsors; a tenth cosponsor was added later, all Democrats [S1][S3][S4].
Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction; that was the bill's last action in the 114th Congress [S5].
The HELP Committee never held a markup, hearing, or floor vote on the bill, and it was never brought to the Senate floor before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in industries with large numbers of first-line supervisors — retail, restaurants, health care, agriculture, and hospitality — continue to benefit from the narrower Vance v. Ball State liability standard, which makes it harder for workers to hold employers responsible for harassment by a boss who directs their daily work but cannot formally hire or fire them. No lawmaker or group is worse off as a result.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers relying on the Vance liability standard

for.name: Sen. Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate.

for.name: 10 of 54 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it its entire Democratic support base in the Senate.

against.name: HELP Committee (no action taken)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled it for a markup, hearing, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. All 10 Senate cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, but no recorded opposition occurred either, since the bill never left committee.

industries.industry: Retail, restaurant, hospitality, and personal-care employers
industries.note: These are the industries the bill's own findings identify as having large numbers of shift leaders who direct daily work without formal hiring-and-firing authority; the bill would make their employers strictly liable for harassment by those workers [S3]. Workers in these industries are the intended beneficiaries. (Record of the bill; industries not separately cited.)

The bill expands strict employer liability beyond harassers with formal hiring-and-firing power and adds a negligence-based liability path, increasing legal exposure and defense costs for employers across all covered sectors [S3].
